analysis.one_liner: Lets a federal board cap "excessive" prices for prescription drugs and medical devices.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in any of its three committees and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a Prescription Drug and Medical Device Price Review Board inside the FDA, made up of the FDA Commissioner and the heads of Medicare, NIH, Defense, and Veterans Affairs. Drug and device makers would have to report their prices and production costs, and the Board would write a formula defining an "excessive" price. Companies charging excessive prices could face civil penalties of up to 10% of sales, a tax on the overcharge, larger Medicaid rebates, and patent terms cut by up to five years, and individuals could legally import cheaper equivalents from approved countries while the overpricing continued. The bill was introduced in the final month of a two-year Congress, sent to three committees, and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and households that buy prescription drugs and medical devices, including the roughly one in four Americans who report difficulty affording medications; Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs that pay drug bills; and anyone petitioning the Board about a drug price.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a five-member federal board with authority to declare a drug or device price "excessive" and bar manufacturers from charging it [S2][S3].
Allows any person to petition the Board for a price determination on a specific drug or device, with a required decision within 90 days [S3].

The price formula must consider production and marketing costs, prices in other countries, federal research investment, patient population size, and whether the price rose more than 2 points above inflation in a quarter [S3].

Enforcement tools include civil penalties up to 10% of gross sales of the product, a tax on the difference between the charged price and the Board's reasonable price, increased Medicaid rebates for up to four rebate periods, and patent terms shortened by up to five years [S2][S3].

If a company is found charging an excessive price, individuals may legally import comparable drugs and devices from countries the Secretary approves as having safety standards at least as protective as U.S. law [S3].
The Board must report excessively priced products to federal agencies each year and recommend they stop paying for them or substitute similar products not sold at excessive prices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of prescription drugs and medical devices, which would face price caps, penalties, a new excise tax, larger Medicaid rebates, shorter patent terms, and competition from parallel imports; critics also warn that reduced returns on new drugs could slow investment in research and development.

drawbacks.text: The bill targets the patents behind high prices — cutting patent terms by up to five years as a penalty — a step critics warn would weaken the exclusivity that funds development of new medicines [S3].

Defining an "excessive" price by regulation is difficult; the Board's formula must weigh cost, therapeutic-class comparisons, foreign prices, and value to patients, and a poorly calibrated formula could penalize genuinely innovative products [S3].

The bill gives a federal board sweeping power over prices across the entire prescription drug and medical device market, including subpoena power and civil penalties, a major expansion of federal economic control that some would oppose on principle [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who pay for medications, the potential benefit is direct and large: a mechanism to force prices toward production costs and to buy equivalents abroad. The main honest cost is the risk that squeezing returns on patented drugs reduces investment in new treatments, and that the enforcement formula is untested and could misfire. The bill's design is aggressive — price caps plus patent cuts plus a tax — which is part of why it drew no Republican support; a narrower version might have advanced further.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with three weeks left in the session, referred to three committees and one subcommittee, and no committee ever considered it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on December 8, 2016, with seven Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees [S5].
On December 22, 2016, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet [S5].
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind appears in the record before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug and medical device manufacturers are better off, since they never faced the price caps, penalties, excess-price tax, larger Medicaid rebates, shortened patents, or personal drug importation the bill would have created. Patients paying high drug prices gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Schakowsky, Doggett, McDermott, Honda, Moore, Kaptur, and Welch

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but no recorded vote ever split the chambers because the bill never left committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would cap their prices at a Board-determined level and add civil penalties, an excess-price excise tax, larger Medicaid rebates, and patent terms cut up to five years for violators. Their gain from the bill dying is patients' continued cost of paying whatever the market bears.
Devices are covered on the same terms as drugs: price reporting, an excessive-price prohibition, penalties, a tax on overcharges, and importation of comparable devices when overpricing is found.
